components.html:
At first glance, any knitting machine seems complicated. Think about the dashboard in a car. There are lots of dials and buttons and levers, but once you learn the names of things you'll quickly discover what you need to make the car go.
Examine the hotspots below and learn the names of the elements that make up your knitting machine. As you work through this course, these terms will be come second-nature and you will associate the terms with the functions of the machine.

  1. Accessory/tools box
  2. Row Counter
  3. Accessory Stand
  4. Punchcard Mechanism
  5. K Carriage (Main Carriage)
  6. Sinker Plate Assembly (presser plate)
  7. Needlebed
  8. Number Strip
  9. Sponge bar
  10. Gate Pegs
  11. Tension Mast

Before you start to set up your machine, identify the tools and accessories that came with your machine.
If you don't have the tools marked "essential" you'll be able to get started knitting, but ask Mr. Google to help you find them.
When looking for tools and fun accessories, keep in mind that this is a Brother/Knit King 9mm machine.
Essential:
  • Table Clamps
  • Needle Pusher
  • Latch Tool
  • Transfer Tools
  • Claw weights
  • Oil (sewing machine oil works great)
Consider Locating:
  • Punchcards and snaps - must have for automatic patterning
  • Carriage lock - good for securing the carriage when packing it
  • Ravel Cord - "must have" for certain techniques
  • Wax - Helps reduce static and makes knitting some yarns easier
  • Single Motif Cams - required for the Single Motif technique
  • Punchcard holder pin - nice but not essential
  • Extra needles - Nice to have on hand - you won't break needles often, but ...

  1. Needle Pusher (1x1)
  2. Machine Oil (lightweight/sewing machine oil)
  3. Ravel cord (Cast on thread)
  4. Yarn Wax
  5. Spare Needles
  6. Punchcards
  7. Latchet (Latch) Tool
  8. Punchcard snaps
  9. Carriage lock (for storing / transporting)
  10. Punch card holder pin
  11. Claw weight(s)
  12. Transfer tools
  13. Table Clamps
  14. Single Motif Cams
If you've mis-placed the Punchcard Holder Pin, don't stress ... most knitters ignore this little accessory.

The 9 mm gauge of this machine allows you to knit with heavier yarns. It is especially good with hand-spun yarns.
You can choose a lighter weight yarn and knit it at a very loose tension for a lightweight fabric. You can knit the same yarn at a tighter tension for a very different look. The fiber, color and texture of the yarn is up to you.
The only limit is the size of the needles. If the yarn is too thick and doesn't fit in the hooks of the needles, it can split and/or jam the machine.

Take a moment to get familiar with the terminology and location of items on the carriage

Don't be overwhelmed by all the buttons, dials and levers on the carriage. As we cover the various techniques available, we will walk through each setting and explore it's impact on your knitting.
Instead of forming each stitch one-at-a-time like in hand knitting, the carriage acts as your hands and fingers.
  • Using the butts of the needle and the channels underneath the carriage, select which needles will knit.

  • The Tension dial controls how the yarn is fed and how large the stitches will be.

  • The Change Knob Tells the machine that you want to knit in pattern

  • The Cam buttons instruct the machine about what type of stitch pattern you want to create
As you continue on your journey to master your machine, all of the other settings will become second nature to you.

To create stitch patterns:
  1. Change Knob
  2. Cam Buttons
  3. Needle Positions (punchcard)

  1. Left Knit Leader Tripper
  2. Right Tripper (Knit Leader and Row Counter)
  3. Tension Dial
  4. Holding Cam Lever
  5. Cam Button Release Lever
  6. Change Knob
  7. Cam Button (Tuck Left)
  8. Cam Button (Tuck Right)
  9. Cam Button(s) (Fairisle and Thread Lace)
  10. Cam Button (Slip Left)
  11. Cam Button (Slip Right)
  12. Sinker Plate Assembly
  13. Yarn Feeder(s)
  14. Yarn Feeder Lever (Gate)
  15. Sinker Plate Knob
  16. Sinker Plate Knob
  17. Tuck Brush(es)
  18. Weaving Brush(es)

Understanding how to set your carriage for PLAIN KNITTING is essential
It is a good habit to always check your carriage settings before starting a new technique or a new piece of knitting. It's easy to have your carriage set for patterning, then come back days later and be surprised that the machine isn't knitting as expected.
Take time every time you sit down to knit and double check the settings.

Save your back, neck and shoulders
In the videos in this course, you'll see me pushing the carriage with one hand. BAD!!!! I'm reaching around the camera.
When you are knitting use both hands and push and pull alternately to move the carriage.
Many knitters also adjust their knitting table so they can stand while knitting.

Arm, hand and wrist position

STOP! LOOK AT THE POSITION OF YOUR HAND AND WRIST IN RELATION TO YOUR ELBOW.Many knitters will find their elbow is below the level of the wrist and hand.
Knitting in this position, after a time, will create an ache and pain through the neck and across the shoulders. Try sitting higher so that your elbow is slightly above the wrist and hand.

More tips

  • A stool for your feet may be needed or your machine table or stand may have to be lowered.

  • If you have a stand to use your machine, the same elbow position is needed. (elbows slightly above the hands)

  • Try standing to knit. Use an adjustable table to keep the elbow position correct. Here's what I use

  • Good lighting is a must

slides.caption:
Some knitters will tie the yarn tail to the table clamp.

You have to remember to remove this as you knit

The manual suggests securing the tail to the cast on comb

Some cast on combs don't have clips and this can be fiddly.

Use a chip clip to not only secure the tail, but it adds a little weight as well.
It's easily removed as you knit.
This method can be used any time you have a yarn tail (knitting stripes).
A spring-type clothes pin works great too!

components.introHtml: No matter what cast on method you use, it's important to secure the yarn tail when casting on so the first few stitches knit correctly.

components.html:
Open Cast on
By definition, an open cast on will have stitches that will unravel if given the chance.
Some machine manuals will give instruction for this type of cast on
The Cast on demonstrated in the previous video is an open cast on.
Here are some variations:
  • Open Cast on with a cast on Comb (shown in the video)
  • Open Cast on with a wire
  • Open Cast on with Ravel cord
Most knitters graduate beyond these methods pretty quickly.
The following cast on methods leave open stitches to be worked later. For example, leave open stitches, then pick them up and hand knit some ribbing. Or turn the knitting, pick up open stitches and knit reverse stockinette.
  • Scrap and Ravel
  • Using a Cast on Rag
You will use these again and again

Closed Cast on
With a closed cast on, the starting stitches are secure.
These techniques can be categorized:
  • Closed but temporary.
    These cast on methods are quick and have their place ... they just wouldn't be appropriate for the finished edge of your next sweater.
    Uses:
    • Cast on for swatching
    • Scrap 'n Ravel Cast on
    • Cut 'n Sew
  • Closed and Functional
    These techniques can be used for the edges of your knitting, without any additional finishing.
    • E-wrap cast on (lots of variations)
    • Chain Cast on

We can knit so much more than plain stockinette with this machine. The punchcard mechanism can automatically create textured and multi-color stitch patterns.
It is critical that you understand the 3 elements that create stitch patterns.
3 settings control stitch patterning:
1
Needle position
2
Change Knob
3
Cam Buttons

1
Needle position
Letters marked on the side of the needlebed A-B-D-E represent:
A Out of Work Position (Non-working Position |NWP) Unused Needles
B Working Position (WP) Needles lined up to knit in stockinette and most stitch patterns
D Middle Position(MP) (Pattern Position) Bring the needles from holding position into working and pattern work positions
E Holding Position (HP) The farthest position from "A" on the needlebed

2
Change Knob
The Change Knob instructs the machine that you are going to be knitting in pattern. This setting COMBINED WITH the Cam Buttons create stitch patterning on your machine.
N Plain Knitting (stockinette) and Lace knitting
KC (Knit Card) for stitch patterns that use needle selection
SM Single Motif
CR Release the carriage from the needlebed

3
Cam Buttons
The Cam Buttons control the action of the needles for specific stitch types.
N / H N="normal"
H=Holds needles in "E" position (both directions)
Plain Releases (cancels) all Cam buttons
Tuck Positions needles for tuck both left and right or independently
MC (Top button only) used for Fairisle Patterns
L (both center buttons) used for knitting with the Lace Carriage
Part Positions needles for SLIP (skip) both left and right or independently

The punchcard mechanism:

1
Card Feeding Button
Push this down to manually rotate the card

2
Punchcard snaps
These snaps hold the card in a circle so it can rotate and repeat the stitch pattern.
Be sure to lap the card so there is no interruption of the pattern and the card flows smoothly in the mechanism

3
Card Lock Lever
3 positions:
  • Double Triangle (the advances with 2 passes of the carriage - double high)
  • Single triangle (the card advances 1 row at a time)
  • Circle: - locked (the card doesn't advance)
4
Card Feeding Knob
Push down and turn to manual advance the card

By setting the Card Lock Lever to the tall (double) triangle, you instruct the punchcard mechanism to expand the stitch pattern design to "double high".
Instead of the card advancing once for each pass of the carriage, the card advances once for every 2 passes of the carriage.
With this setting, this stitch pattern is distorted which can produce interesting results WITHOUT punching a new card.
This technique can be applied to other stitch pattern types, slip, weaving, etc. Care should be taken with tuck stitch, too many tucks can cause problems.

How to cancel the working of end needle selection mechanism

Your machine selects needles based on your punchcard pattern. Depending on the pattern and the number of needles in work, the needles on each end of the knitting may be selected. This may or may not be what you want.
The following video discusses the impact of end needle selection with Fairisle, but this also impacts other stitch patterns as well. For example when working tuck, if the end needle is selected and the stitch tucks, it will be more difficult to seam that edge.
With Thread Lace, you may get a long float as shown in the video.
This machine has a setting under the carriage that allows you to cancel the end needle selection as needed.
Use a single prong transfer tool to switch the end needle selection cams as needed for your chosen stitch pattern.
Page 42
of your manual discusses this setting
Watch the video at {2:34} for an alternate solution to this problem.

The Brother 260 came with a set of punchcards and the manual refers to them by number.
  • Full Size punchcard images
    • Download, print and punch your own cards
  • Original Scans
    • Here are the original scans for your reference

Tuck is a great way
to add texture and interest to your knitting.
When knitting tuck, certain needles do not knit and the working yarn travels OVER the needles out of work.
Once you understand how tuck stitch is created on your machine, the sky's the limit!
  • Change the number of rows tucked
  • Change the needles selected
  • Change the number of rows between tucks
  • Put some needles out of work
  • Add color
  • Mix 'n match stitch patterns
Check out the Knit it Now Stitch Browser for Tuck and Tuck lace Inspiration! Here are a few samples:

Your manual (pages 20-24) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for tuck.

  1. Cast on and knit a few rows in plain stockinette
  2. End with the carriage on the left
  3. Insert the card an lockon row 1 - rotate card to the start line
  4. Set the ard lever to the ● mark
  5. Set the Change Knob to "KC" (knit card)
  6. Move the carriage slowly to the right (needles are selected to "D" position)
  7. Push the cam buttons for ◀ tuck ▶
  8. Set the card lock to the ▼ mark
  9. Begin Knitting

For more about Slip Stitch, visit:
the Knit it Now Classroom: Slip Stitch

Slip Stitch is a great way
to add texture and interest to your knitting.
When knitting slip, certain needles do not knit and the working yarn travels UNDER the needles.
Once you understand how slip stitch is created on your machine, the sky's the limit!
  • Change the number of rows slipped
  • Change the needles selected
  • Change the number of rows between slipped stitches
  • Put some needles out of work
  • Add color
  • Mix 'n match stitch patterns
Check out the Knit it Now Stitch Library for Slip and Multi-Color Slip Stitch inspiration!

Your manual (pages 26-26) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for Slip Stitch.
  1. Knit several rows in plain stockinette, end with the carriage on the left
  2. Insert the punch card and set the card lock lever to ●
  3. Hang claw weights
  4. Set the Change Knob to the "KC" position (knit card)
  5. Pass the carriage to the right. Needles are selected in "D" Position
  6. Push both Part buttons in
  7. Set the card lock lever to the ▼ mark
  8. Pass the carriage to the right and continue knitting

The often over-looked technique of Knitweave creates beautiful knitted fabrics with lots of possibilities.
Unlike traditional weaving, think of weaving on the machine as "laying-in" a second yarn on top of the knitting.
It is a decorative technique that can be used to create interesting textures and incorporate yarn that may not be suitable for your machine.
Have a small amount thick, fancy (possibly expensive) yarn? Use it in your machine knitting with Knitweave!
Check out the Knit it Now Stitch Browser for Knit Weave inspiration!

Knitting 2 colors in a row with one pass of the carriage is known as Fairisle. When machine knitting place both colors in the yarn feeder of the carriage, let the punchcard instruct the machine to select needles and both colors will knit as instructed.
Tell a hand knitter that you can knit a fairisle hat in an afternoon and they will be amazed.
(PLUS your fairisle will look sooooo much better than hand knitting. )
Check out the Knit it Now Stitch Browser for Fairisle inspiration!
Your manual (pages 31-38) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for Fairisle.

Knitting 2 colors in the same row
  1. Thread the carriage with one end of yarn in the "A: feeder
  2. Knit several rows in plain stockinette, ending with the carriage on the left
  3. Insert a punchcard and set the lever to the ● mark
  4. Set the Change Knob to "KC" (knit card) and move the carraige from left to right (needles will be selected)
  5. Push in the Upper MC button
  6. Set the card lock lever to ▼
  7. Thread teh second yarn end into yarn feeder "B" (without opening the gate)
  8. Push the carriage to the left while holding the yarn with your left hand
  9. Continue Knitting

Often overlooked, Thread Lace is an easy technique to create openwork "lace" fabrics.
It's not fairisle, it's not true lace, but it's a unique stitch pattern that can create beautiful knit fabrics.
Knit with a thick yarn and a very fine yarn, there are lots of possibilities with your machine
NOTE:
Thread lace is knitting is very similar to Fairisle knitting with 2 differences:
  1. Choose a stitch pattern with short floats (1-2 stitches) The yarn is carried behind the "lace" openings. If the floats are too long, the appearance of lace is lost

  2. Press in BOTH MC buttons for Thread Lace. (Fairisle uses only the top MC button)
Your manual (pages 31-38) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for Fairisle.

Knit 2 strands of yarn together and let the machine position them so you view one color on one side of the knitting and the 2nd color on the other side of the knitting.
This technique is also called Platting or Plating.
This technique can be used on both the single and double bed. It's a great way to bulk up finer yarns and play with color and texture


Watch the video below to learn about plaiting. (Jump to {02:08} for Brother 260-specific information.)

Picture this:
  • You have a knitting machine with 100+ needles.
  • You use a carriage to quickly knit 100+ needles with the pass of the carriage
  • Imagine cloning that needlebed, turning it 180° and positioning the needles facing each other.

Now you have a setup that can not only create purl stitches, but knit stitches as well. That is the basic idea of a knitting machine ribber.
Imagine being able to knit k1, p1 ribbing with the pass of the carriage ... but wait! There's so much more!

A bit of advice:
If you are just getting started with machine knitting and have a ribber, be kind to yourself and take this advice.
Put the ribber aside for a while ... master the single bed BEFORE adding the ribber to the equation.
Learn and understand the settings for your machine. Practice with a few different yarns, learn to read and follow patterns ... get some successes under your belt before adding the ribber.
Trust me .... been there ... done that

components.html:
Don't forget the Ribber Cast on Comb!

A ribber cast on comb is essential, not only for casting on, but for adding even weight on your knitting. The weight is critical for proper formation of the stitches when knitting on a double bed.

When using the ribber, position the mast so it's leaning toward you.
  • Look for the bend in the lower section of the mast
  • Turn it as shown in the video
  • Swivel the yarn guide to the back
  • Rotate the tension mast assembly

When working on the main bed only, reverse the setup so the mast is leaning away from you.
This is not critical, but the most important thing is that your yarn flows smoothly no matter how you set up the mast.

• Connecting Pin
    Connects the ribber carriage to the main bed connecting arm

  • Cam Lever This lever has 2 positions:
    P.R.: The needles don't knit (for circular knitting or for the selvage) Similar to slip
    N: The needles knit for normal knitting

  • Tucking Lever This lever has 2 positions:
    P: For tuck stitch (English Rib, Fisherman's Rib)
    R: For Normal and Circular Knitting
  • Holding Cam Lever
    • This lever has 2 positions:
    =: For Normal knitting
    -: For partial knitting (short rows / hold) The needles in "E" position don't knit
  • Tension Dial
    • Controls the flow of yarn to the ribber needles. Impacts stitch size and gauge
  • Slide Lever
    • This lever has 2 positions: I: for a looser stitch
    II: for a tighter stitch (2 for tiny)
Adjust the ribber side to side: loosen the 2 screws on the left.

Racking refers to the position of the ribber needles in relation to the main bed needles.
"P" Pitch: Needles are directly across from each other.
"H" Half Pitch: Needles alternate
"Swinging" the ribber can be used in cast on methods as well as for creating beautiful and unusual knit and purl stitch patterns.
On the Brother 260, racking one number means turning the racking handle 2 clicks.
A ribber cast on comb is essential, not only for casting on, but for adding even weight on your knitting. The weight is critical for proper formation of the stitches when knitting on a double bed.
Your ribber manual (pages 18-24) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for a basic 1x1 cast on.

The full needle rib technique uses all needles on the ribber and main bed at the same time. It is used to create beautiful reversible fabrics and often used to create multi-color double bed jacquard
For success with this technique, it is CRITICAL that you understand the concept of Full vs Half pitch (the position of the needles of both beds)

Another variation of Full Needle Rib is Flat Rib. Instead of all needles being in work, selected needles on either the main bed or ribber are put into work, creating knit stitch texture against a purl background.

English Rib (also known as Half Fisherman Rib) is a 1x1 rib variation with stitches tucking every other row on one bed (either the ribber or the main bed).
This technique produces a wide, thick, stretchy fabric that has many uses.
This video explores tuck on each bed and gives tips for making the edges of your knitting beautiful.

components.html: Similar to English Rib, Fisherman Rib is a wide, thick, stretchy fabric knit in a 1x1 needle arrangement with tuck stitch on BOTH needlebeds.

Settings:
Ribber:
  • Tucking Lever: P
    • Settings:
    Ribber:
    • Tucking Lever: P
    • LEFT Cam Lever up P-R
    Main Bed:
    • Change Knob: N
    • Right Tuck Cam button engaged (in)

    With the setting shown above, the beds alternate tucking. As one bed tucks, the other knits:

Ribber Main Bed
Carriage on the right, knit left Tuck Knit
Carriage on the left, knit right: Knit Tuck
Carriage on the right, knit left Tuck Knit
Carriage on the left, knit right: Knit Tuck

This machine comes with a D-Slider The Drop Stitch Lace technique can also be worked by simply manually dropping the loops.
NOTE: Although this is referred to as "lace" there are no eyelets formed. The "lace" effect is subtle, but adds pretty texture to the knit side.
Overview of Drop-Stitch lace
  • MAIN BED
    • Selected needles do not form stitches, they just hold loops
    • Carriage is set to slip in both directions (both part buttons remain engaged)
    • Change Knob to KC
    • Cancel the End Needle Selection
    • Punchcard must have 1 unpunched row before punched row
  • RIBBER
    • All knitting takes place on the ribber
    • Carriage set for plain knitting
Knitting Sequence
  1. Carriage on the right. Knit to the left.
    • Ribber stitches knit
    • Needles are SELECTED on the main bed

  2. Carriage on the left. Knit to the right.
    • Ribber stitches knit.
    • Loops are formed on the selected needles
    • AND needles are selected according to the pattern

  3. Engage the D-Slider and drop the loops

  4. Remover the D-Slider
This sequence repeats for the length of the knitting
